 The painkiller that could turn dengue deadly
 Published : 22 November 2026
 • 
 Updated : 22 November 2026, 00:13
 • 
 HEALTH
 SHARE 
 Prof Dr Mohammad Azizur Rahman
 Prof Dr Kaushik Ghosh
 Prof Dr Mohammad Azizur Rahman 
 and
 Prof Dr Kaushik Ghosh 
 A fever strikes, the body aches, and the first instinct is often to reach for a painkiller. But during dengue season, that seemingly harmless decision could have dangerous consequences. One familiar medicine, aspirin, can turn an already worrying illness into a medical emergency.
 Dengue, spread through the bite of an infected mosquito, often begins with high fever, severe headache, pain behind the eyes, aching joints, nausea and sometimes a rash. While most people recover with rest and proper care, some develop serious complications, including dangerous bleeding.
 Tap here to add The Daily Star as a trusted source 
 This is where aspirin becomes a hidden threat. Aspirin interferes with the blood’s natural ability to stop bleeding. Dengue can already reduce the number of blood cells responsible for preventing blood loss. Combining the two increases the risk of bleeding from the nose or gums, blood in vomit or stools, and potentially life-threatening internal bleeding.
 The warning extends beyond aspirin. Common painkillers such as ibuprofen, diclofenac and naproxen should also be avoided when dengue is suspected.
 So, what should someone with dengue take? Paracetamol, taken according to a doctor’s advice, is generally the safer option for managing fever and pain. Drinking sufficient fluids, including water, oral rehydration drinks and soup, alongside adequate rest, supports recovery. However, medication alone is not enough. Recognising danger signs can save lives.
 Severe stomach pain, repeated vomiting, unusual bleeding, rapid breathing, extreme weakness, drowsiness or cold, clammy skin demand immediate medical attention. Importantly, a falling blood cell count is not the only warning. Doctors also assess blood pressure, fluid loss and the patient’s overall condition.
 Contrary to popular belief, patients do not automatically need blood cell transfusions simply because their counts fall. Unnecessary transfusions may cause harm.
 Prevention remains equally important. Empty standing water from flowerpots, buckets and discarded containers weekly, use mosquito repellents and wear protective clothing.
 In Bangladesh, where dengue remains a recurring public health concern, awareness must begin at home.
 The message is simple: When dengue is suspected, think twice before swallowing a painkiller. Seek medical advice early, avoid aspirin and remember that one small tablet can make a dangerous difference.
 The writers are Professor Dr Mohammad Azizur Rahman, Visiting Professor, Sree Balaji Medical College, Chennai, India, and Professor Dr Kaushik Ghosh, Head of Medicine, Raiganj Government Medical College, West Bengal, India. Email: [email protected] ; [email protected]
